summary: Conflict between Russia and Ukraine began in 2014, when Russia seized and annexed Crimea and backed separatists in the eastern Donbas region. On 24 February 2022 Russia launched a full-scale invasion from the north, east and south, which President Vladimir Putin called a 'special military operation'. Ukrainian resistance defeated the attack on Kyiv, and Russian forces withdrew from the north in April, leaving evidence of war crimes. Russia took Mariupol and much of the south-east, but Ukrainian counteroffensives in late 2022 recaptured large areas around Kharkiv and Kherson. Russia declared the annexation of four Ukrainian regions in September 2022, a move rejected internationally. In 2023 Russia took Bakhmut and a Ukrainian counteroffensive made little progress; in 2024 Russian forces advanced slowly in the east, while Ukraine launched an incursion into Russia's Kursk region, where North Korean troops joined the fighting. In 2023 the International Criminal Court issued an arrest warrant for Putin. The war continues, with Russia occupying about a fifth of Ukraine.
casualties: Military killed and wounded are estimated in the hundreds of thousands on each side, and the UN had verified at least 12,340 civilian deaths by 30 November 2024, a figure it says is an undercount.

brief.hook: Russia seized Crimea in 2014 and backed rebels in Donbas; in February 2022 it launched a full-scale invasion to bring Ukraine to heel.

sides.who: Ukraine's armed forces and volunteers, armed and funded by the United States, European countries and other partners
Russia's army, with mercenaries such as the Wagner Group, troops from occupied Donbas and, from late 2024, some 11,000–12,000 North Korean soldiers

brief.resultLine: At the end of 2024 the war was still being fought, with Russia holding roughly a fifth of Ukraine and pressing slow, costly attacks in the east.

strategies.name: Holding Kyiv with artillery
strategies.text: Russia bet on taking Kyiv in days and had no fallback plan. Massed fire from Ukrainian artillery stalled the columns north of the city, and by early April they had pulled back.

strategies.name: Striking the supply lines
strategies.text: With Western long-range weapons, Ukraine hit Russian depots and the bridges over the Dnipro. Cut off from supplies, Russian troops abandoned Kherson's west bank in November 2022.

strategies.name: Fortified lines and attrition
strategies.text: Russia built the deepest minefields and trench lines seen in Europe since 1945, which halted Ukraine's 2023 counteroffensive. Its own assaults then gained ground only slowly, at a heavy cost in lives.

impact: By late 2024 some 6.7 million Ukrainians were refugees abroad, and about 3.7 million more were displaced at home.
Military dead and wounded ran into the hundreds of thousands, by most estimates, though neither side publishes full figures.
Finland joined NATO in 2023 and Sweden in 2024, abandoning long traditions of staying out of military alliances.
Cheap drones and dense minefields reshaped war on land, making large breakthroughs very hard for either side.

details: After massing between 169,000 and 190,000 troops on Ukraine's borders, including in Belarus, Putin recognised the independence of the two Russian-backed separatist entities in eastern Ukraine on 21 February 2022. They had been at war with Ukrainian forces since 2014. The next day Russia sent troops into the areas they held, describing them as peacekeepers. Western governments responded with the first new sanctions.

At dawn on 24 February Putin announced a 'special military operation', and missile strikes hit cities across Ukraine. Russian forces advanced from Belarus towards Kyiv, from the north-east towards Kharkiv, and from Crimea into the south. Airborne troops attacked Hostomel airfield near the capital. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy declared martial law and general mobilisation and stayed in Kyiv, and millions of Ukrainians began to flee.

Russian forces encircled Mariupol, a port city on the Sea of Azov, in the first days of the war and subjected it to constant bombardment, cutting off water, power and food. On 16 March an airstrike destroyed the city's drama theatre, where hundreds of civilians were sheltering; the word 'children' had been painted in large letters outside. The UN confirmed 1,348 civilian deaths in the siege and believes the real toll is thousands higher.

The advance on Kyiv stalled in early March, and a Ukrainian counteroffensive from late March forced Russian forces to withdraw from the north, completed by 7 April. When Ukrainian troops re-entered the suburb of Bucha on 1 April they found bodies of civilians in the streets. The UN documented at least 73 unlawful killings there, with more under investigation; Ukrainian authorities recovered 458 bodies. Russia denied responsibility.

The last Ukrainian defenders of Mariupol held out for weeks in the tunnels of the Azovstal steelworks. After evacuations of civilians and wounded soldiers, the remaining troops surrendered, the last on 20 May, and Russia took full control of the ruined city. Its capture gave Russia a land corridor from the Donbas to Crimea. In the summer Russian forces also took Sievierodonetsk and Lysychansk in Luhansk region.

Russia's blockade of Ukraine's Black Sea ports had trapped millions of tonnes of grain and pushed up world food prices. On 22 July Ukraine and Russia signed separate agreements with Turkey and the UN in Istanbul, allowing grain ships to sail through a protected corridor. The deal let Ukraine resume large-scale exports. Russia briefly suspended its participation in October 2022 and finally withdrew on 17 July 2023, after which Ukraine kept shipping grain through its own corridor.

On 6 September Ukrainian forces, equipped with Western-supplied weapons including HIMARS rocket launchers, broke through thinly held Russian lines in Kharkiv region. Within days they had retaken Balakliia, Kupiansk and the logistics hub of Izium, recapturing thousands of square kilometres. It was the largest Ukrainian gain since the defence of Kyiv. On 21 September Putin announced a partial mobilisation of 300,000 reservists, and many Russian men fled abroad to avoid the call-up.

After referendums held under occupation and condemned as shams by Ukraine and Western governments, Putin announced on 30 September the annexation of Donetsk, Luhansk, Kherson and Zaporizhzhia regions, even though Russian forces did not control all of them. The UN General Assembly later declared the annexations invalid, and Ukraine and its allies regard them as illegal. Russia had already annexed Crimea in 2014 after a disputed referendum.

Kherson was the only regional capital Russia had captured since February. After months of Ukrainian strikes on bridges and supply lines across the Dnipro, Russia announced a withdrawal to the river's east bank, and Ukrainian troops entered the city on 11 November to celebrations. The retreat left all territory west of the Dnipro in Ukrainian hands, but the city remained within range of Russian artillery across the river and was shelled for the rest of the war.

The battle for Bakhmut, a small city in Donetsk region, became the longest and bloodiest of the war. Russia's Wagner Group, a private military company that recruited heavily among prisoners, led months of costly assaults. Wagner claimed full control on 20 May 2023 and Russia declared victory the next day. US officials estimated that Russia suffered about 100,000 casualties in the battle.

In early June Ukraine launched a long-awaited counteroffensive, mainly in Zaporizhzhia and Donetsk regions, aiming to cut the land corridor to Crimea. Its brigades, many trained and equipped by NATO countries, ran into deep minefields, trenches and drones in Russia's prepared defences. After months of fighting and heavy losses on both sides, Ukraine had regained only a few villages, and by late 2023 the front was again largely static.

Early on 6 June the Kakhovka Dam on the Dnipro, then held by Russian forces, was breached, draining its huge reservoir and flooding towns and villages downstream on both banks. About 600 square kilometres were flooded, and dozens to hundreds of people died, many in the Russian-occupied town of Oleshky. Most independent analysts attribute the breach to Russian forces; Russia denied responsibility and blamed Ukraine.

After months of feuding with Russia's defence ministry, Wagner leader Yevgeny Prigozhin led his fighters in a brief armed rebellion on 23–24 June, seizing the military headquarters in Rostov-on-Don and advancing towards Moscow. A deal brokered by Belarus ended the mutiny within a day. Prigozhin was killed when his plane crashed two months later. The mutiny exposed divisions in Russia's war effort, and Wagner's fighters were absorbed into other forces.

With Western military aid delayed and Ukrainian forces short of artillery ammunition, Russia regained the initiative. After months of attacks, Ukrainian troops withdrew from the fortified town of Avdiivka, near Donetsk city, which Russian forces captured on 17 February 2024. It was Russia's largest gain since Bakhmut. Russian forces then advanced slowly westward towards the town of Pokrovsk through the year, at heavy cost in men and equipment.

On 10 May Russian forces crossed the border into northern Kharkiv region, attacking towards Vovchansk and opening a new front that stretched Ukraine's defences. The advance was halted within weeks, after the United States allowed Ukraine to strike Russian forces just across the border with American weapons, but Kharkiv city, Ukraine's second largest, remained under heavy missile and glide-bomb attack throughout the year.

On 6 August about 11,000 Ukrainian troops crossed into Russia's Kursk region, seizing the town of Sudzha and hundreds of square kilometres: the largest foreign attack on Russian territory since the Second World War. Ukraine hoped to divert Russian forces from the Donbas and gain a bargaining chip. Russia assembled around 78,000 troops to push the Ukrainians back, and the fighting in Kursk continued into 2025.

About 10,000–12,000 North Korean soldiers were sent to Russia in autumn 2024, arriving in the Kursk region in late October, and the first clashes with Ukrainian forces were reported in early November. Russia and North Korea acknowledged the deployment only in April 2025. At the end of 2024 the war continued, with Russia occupying about a fifth of Ukraine's territory.
